RL-Guided Temporal Localization for Dual-Channel Retrieval in Long-Horizon Agent Memory

Dabin Sheng Affiliation: Key Laboratory of Pervasive Computing, Ministry of EducationDepartment of Computer Science and Technology, Tsinghua University    Zhe Wu Affiliation: Key Laboratory of Pervasive Computing, Ministry of EducationDepartment of Computer Science and Technology, Tsinghua University    Jinming Zhao Affiliation: Qiyuan Lab    Junliang Xing ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: Key Laboratory of Pervasive Computing, Ministry of EducationDepartment of Computer Science and Technology, Tsinghua University    Yuanchun Shi Email: {sdb26,wu-z24}@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn{jlxing,shiyc}@tsinghua.edu.cn  zhaojinming@qiyuanlab.com Affiliation: Key Laboratory of Pervasive Computing, Ministry of EducationDepartment of Computer Science and Technology, Tsinghua University
Abstract

Time-aware retrieval is crucial for long-horizon LLM agents to effectively leverage ever-growing long-term memory. Existing methods focus on lexical or semantic similarity, leading to target memories being crowded out by temporally mismatched yet semantically similar candidates. Even time-aware approaches inject temporal cues only during memory organization or answer generation, overlooking temporal constraints at the retrieval stage, where candidate selection occurs—the root cause of the displacement. Inspired by the temporal contiguity effect in human episodic memory, we propose TIDER (Temporal Interval-driven Dual-channel Evidence Retrieval), a time-aware agentic retrieval framework. Central to TIDER is a reinforcement learning (RL)-trained temporal interval locator that infers the temporal windows in which the evidence lies. RL optimizes window localization as a discrete, non-differentiable retrieval decision, using composite rewards to convert sparse answer supervision into fine-grained retrieval feedback. These temporal windows first define the temporal retrieval channel; the retrieved candidates are then merged with results from the semantic channel and reranked by proximity to the windows. This temporal grounding enables TIDER to retrieve temporally aligned evidence that would otherwise be drowned out by the volume of semantically similar yet temporally mismatched memories. With a lightweight 1.7B locator, TIDER achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on both long-horizon memory benchmarks—61.52% on LifeBench (+8.82%) and 78.96% on LoCoMo (+3.66%), which indicates that temporal cues are crucial for pinpointing target evidence amid a vast pool of semantically similar historical events in long-term daily-life memory.

1 Introduction

In recent years, long-term personalized assistants powered by large language model agents have advanced rapidly [16, 18, 14, 2, 34]. Sustaining such long-horizon interactions requires a foundational capability: retrieving pertinent evidence from an ever-growing history of daily events to address user queries [5, 10]. However, daily events are highly homogeneous in surface semantics—“had dinner with family” can recur hundreds of times within a year—and the cue that genuinely tells one occurrence from another is often when it took place. This makes time-aware retrieval the central bottleneck: the system must locate the right evidence among many semantically similar events recurring at different times. In long-horizon personalized memory benchmarks such as LifeBench [4] and ATM-Bench [17], 80–90% of questions involve temporal expressions such as “what did I have for lunch after returning from Japan?”, making time-aware retrieval indispensable rather than incidental.

Existing agentic memory systems incorporate temporal information mostly outside the retrieval stage. Some inject temporal cues during memory organization with timestamps, temporal knowledge graphs, or time-aware structures [11, 21, 26]; others strengthen temporal reasoning during answer generation with neuro-symbolic reasoning, program solvers, or temporal operators [7, 25, 13, 29]; recent RL-based methods optimize memory operations or post-retrieval candidate filtering [31, 27, 6]. None of these methods addresses the root cause: once the correct evidence has been crowded out at retrieval, downstream reasoning and post-retrieval filtering can only operate on an incomplete or contaminated candidate set. Borrowing prior time-aware retrieval is also a poor fit: rule-based normalizers [33] fail on personal, fuzzy phrasings such as “the week of her birthday”, while time-sensitive encoders [1, 28, 20] couple temporal and semantic signals in one vector space, demanding extra supervision and degrading semantic recall. Long-term memory, therefore, calls for a retrieval-stage, query-adaptive temporal mechanism decoupled from the semantic encoder.

Motivated by the temporal contiguity effect in human episodic memory, where retrieval is shaped by temporal distance as well as semantic association [9], we propose TIDER (Temporal Interval-driven Dual-channel Evidence Retrieval), a time-aware agentic retrieval framework for long-term memory; the basic idea is illustrated in Figure 1. TIDER decouples temporal cues from the semantic encoder and represents them as temporal windows at the retrieval stage. Central to TIDER is a temporal interval locator πθ\pi_{\theta} trained via reinforcement learning: given a query and a timeline summary, πθ\pi_{\theta} decides whether the query is time-sensitive and predicts the windows that contain the target evidence. Window localization is a discrete, non-differentiable decision, so we cast it as an RL problem. The predicted windows define an independent temporal retrieval channel, while the semantic retrieval channel runs in parallel. Results from the two channels are merged and reranked by their distance to the predicted windows, promoting temporally aligned evidence into the top-kk and suppressing semantically close but temporally mismatched distractors. πθ\pi_{\theta} is trained under a composite reward over temporal need, window localization, evidence coverage, and answer correctness. When the query is non-temporal, πθ\pi_{\theta} closes the temporal channel, and TIDER falls back to the semantic retrieval.

We evaluate TIDER on LifeBench [4] and LoCoMo [15], where it consistently outperforms prior agentic memory frameworks, time-aware retrieval methods, and temporal reasoning methods, with the largest gains on hard queries that require distinguishing semantically similar events recurring at different times. Our contributions are:

  1. 1.

    A time-aware agentic retrieval framework for long-term memory. TIDER predicts query-adaptive temporal windows that define a temporal channel parallel to the semantic one, and reranks merged candidates by window distance, resolving the bottleneck that semantically similar events from different times are hard to distinguish at retrieval.

  2. 2.

    A reinforcement-learning algorithm for training the temporal interval locator. Rewards over temporal need, window localization, evidence coverage, and answer correctness convert sparse answer-only supervision into fine-grained retrieval-stage feedback, enabling the locator to predict evidence-covering windows that improve downstream retrieval.

  3. 3.

    State-of-the-art performance on long-horizon memory benchmarks. With only a 1.7B locator, TIDER reaches 61.52% on LifeBench (+8.82%+8.82\%) and 78.96% on LoCoMo (+3.66%+3.66\%), indicating that temporal cues are crucial for pinpointing target evidence amid a vast pool of semantically similar historical events in long-term daily-life memory.

2 Related Work

2.1 Long-term Agentic Memory

Long-term agentic memory is an active area of research for LLM agents. One line focuses on the organization of memories: MemGPT [19] virtualizes context paging, A-MEM [30] maintains a Zettelkasten-style dynamic index, Mem0 [5] and MemoryBank [35] extract and consolidate episodic facts, Zep [21] encodes events as a temporal knowledge graph with explicit validity intervals, and TiMem [11] builds a multi-granularity temporal tree. Another line applies reinforcement learning to memory operations: Memory-R1 [31] and Mem-α\alpha [27] train policies with GRPO [23] to decide when to create or update memory, while Memory-T1 [6] applies RL to multi-session temporal reasoning at the answer stage. All of these methods act either upstream of retrieval (deciding what to store and when to update) or downstream (filtering candidates after retrieval), and none directly optimizes the retrieval stage itself. TIDER fills this gap by applying reinforcement learning to the generation of retrieval-time temporal constraints rather than to memory operations or post-retrieval reasoning.

2.2 Time-aware Retrieval and Temporal Reasoning

Conventional time-aware retrieval models temporal signals inside a vector space: TempRetriever [1] trains separate temporal and semantic encoders, TsContriever [28] trains a temporal query encoder with a temporal-need gate, TSM [8] merges multiple time-specifier-conditioned retrievers, and TimeR4 [20] trains temporal embedders or rerankers over temporal knowledge graphs. Coupling temporal and semantic signals within a single feature space requires large-scale temporal supervision and degrades semantic recall. Heuristic-based methods such as MRAG [33] instead split the query into temporal and semantic parts and rely on hand-crafted templates or date-distance scoring; they cannot parse relative or fuzzy personal-history phrasings such as “the week of her birthday”. In contrast, TIDER’s temporal windows live outside any vector space: the locator emits explicit temporal windows that constrain an independent temporal channel, leaving the semantic encoder untouched. A complementary line strengthens downstream temporal reasoning given retrieved evidence: TReMu [7] translates evidence into Python via neuro-symbolic reasoning, CoTime [29] uses SQL-style temporal operators, and NeSTR [13] performs neuro-symbolic abductive reasoning over symbolic temporal relations. These methods take the retrieved set as given and ask how to compute over it, while we ask the upstream question of whether the retrieved set covers the correct temporal windows at all.

3 Method

TIDER is a time-aware agentic retrieval framework for long-term memory QA that decouples temporal constraints from the semantic embedding space and expresses them as explicit temporal windows. The pipeline is built around a reinforcement-learned locator πθ\pi_{\theta}: given a query and a timeline summary, πθ\pi_{\theta} predicts the windows that contain the required evidence (Section 3.1). The predicted windows define an independent temporal channel that runs in parallel with the always-on semantic channel, and the merged candidates are reranked by their temporal distance to the predicted windows (Section 3.2). The locator is trained with a composite reward over temporal need, window localization, evidence coverage, and answer correctness (Section 3.3). When the query is non-temporal, πθ\pi_{\theta} closes the temporal channel, and TIDER falls back to the semantic retrieval.

3.1 Temporal Constraint Generation

TIDER takes a user’s multi-turn dialogue history 𝒞\mathcal{C} and a query qq as input, and produces an evidence set ℰ^\hat{\mathcal{E}} for a downstream LLM, which generates an answer a^\hat{a} conditioned on ℰ^\hat{\mathcal{E}} and compared against the gold answer a∗a^{*}. This subsection describes the two steps that turn 𝒞\mathcal{C} into the inputs consumed at the retrieval stage: first, the dialogue is compressed into a temporally anchored event memory pool ℳ\mathcal{M}, then a locator πθ\pi_{\theta} rewrites the query’s temporal need into an explicit temporal localization zz.

We convert the raw dialogue 𝒞\mathcal{C} into a temporally anchored event memory pool, so that events sharing a temporal neighborhood and semantic similarity are explicitly grouped into the same cluster and become amenable to window-based retrieval:

ℳ={mi=(di,si,ℐi)}i=1N,\mathcal{M}=\{m_{i}=(d_{i},s_{i},\mathcal{I}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}, (1)

where di=[distart,diend]d_{i}=[d_{i}^{\text{start}},d_{i}^{\text{end}}] is cluster ii’s date span, taken as the union of its members’ timestamps; sis_{i} is the cluster’s event summary; and ℐi\mathcal{I}_{i} is the set of raw memory items inside the cluster. The construction is performed by an LLM that extracts items with timestamps from each dialogue turn, then clusters them first by date and then by semantic similarity; Appendix B provides the construction details and corpus-level cluster statistics.

Implicit or relative temporal phrasings such as “the week of her birthday” or “after the last get-together” are hard to cover with rule templates and hurt semantic retrieval when forced into a shared embedding. We therefore introduce a locator πθ(⋅∣q,𝒮q)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q,\mathcal{S}_{q}) that takes the query qq together with a query-adaptive timeline summary 𝒮q={(di,si)}i∈𝒩q⊆ℳ\mathcal{S}_{q}=\{(d_{i},s_{i})\}_{i\in\mathcal{N}_{q}}\subseteq\mathcal{M}, and emits a structured temporal localization

z=(detect,Wpred),Wpred={wℓ=[wℓstart,wℓend]}ℓ=1L,z=(\texttt{detect},W_{\text{pred}}),\qquad W_{\text{pred}}=\{w_{\ell}=[w_{\ell}^{\text{start}},w_{\ell}^{\text{end}}]\}_{\ell=1}^{L}, (2)

where detect∈{true,false}\texttt{detect}\in\{\text{true},\text{false}\} gates the temporal channel and WpredW_{\text{pred}} is a set of temporal windows where the evidence may lie. Because the constraint is expressed as explicit windows rather than vectors, TIDER neither needs to train a time-sensitive encoder nor contaminates the semantic embedding; πθ\pi_{\theta} is trained via GRPO [23] under the composite reward of Section 3.3.

With ℳ\mathcal{M} from preprocessing and zz from the locator, TIDER’s retrieval can be formalized as a scoring function conditioned on the temporal localization,

f:(q,ℳ,z)↦ℰ^,f:(q,\mathcal{M};z)\mapsto\hat{\mathcal{E}}, (3)

whose computation is described in Section 3.2: it uses detect and WpredW_{\text{pred}} inside zz to drive parallel semantic and temporal recalls, merges their candidates, and reranks the merged set by date distance to WpredW_{\text{pred}}, yielding the final top-kk set ℰ^\hat{\mathcal{E}}.

3.2 Dual-channel Constrained Retrieval

A single-channel retriever cannot balance semantic and temporal evidence: a semantic-only channel floods the top-kk with semantically similar events from wrong times, while a temporal-only channel misses temporally distant yet relevant evidence. TIDER therefore runs the two channels in parallel and merges their candidates. The semantic channel encodes the query qq and each memory mim_{i} into vectors 𝐞q\mathbf{e}_{q} and 𝐞mi\mathbf{e}_{m_{i}} via the dense retriever and uses their cosine similarity as the semantic score,

sem​(q,mi)=𝐞q⊤​𝐞mi‖𝐞q‖​‖𝐞mi‖,\text{sem}(q,m_{i})=\frac{\mathbf{e}_{q}^{\top}\mathbf{e}_{m_{i}}}{\|\mathbf{e}_{q}\|\,\|\mathbf{e}_{m_{i}}\|}, (4)

The temporal channel is gated by detect: when detect=false\texttt{detect}=\text{false}, it is closed and retrieval degrades to only semantic; when detect=true\texttt{detect}=\text{true}, for each mi∈ℳm_{i}\in\mathcal{M} we check whether its temporal window did_{i} overlaps any window in WpredW_{\text{pred}} and keep only the overlapping candidates.

The candidates from the two channels are unified by a single ranking score that combines (i) the semantic similarity, (ii) a boost for entering the temporal channel, and (iii) a temporal distance decay that suppresses semantically-close but temporally-mismatched distractors:

score(q,mi)=γ(disti)⋅[sem(q,mi)+λboost⋅[mi∈temporal channel]],\text{score}(q,m_{i})=\gamma(\text{dist}_{i})\cdot\bigl[\,\text{sem}(q,m_{i})+\lambda_{\text{boost}}\cdot\mathbf{1}\!\left[m_{i}\in\text{temporal channel}\right]\,\bigr], (5)

Here disti\text{dist}_{i} denotes the smallest date distance from mim_{i}’s event date did_{i} to WpredW_{\text{pred}}: zero when did_{i} overlaps any window, and the number of days to the nearest window boundary otherwise. The coefficient γ\gamma takes a piecewise form with no decay inside a buffer, linear decay outside the buffer:

γ⁡(disti)={1,disti≤τbuf,max⁡(γmin, 1−ρ⁡(disti−τbuf)),disti>τbuf.\gamma(\text{dist}_{i})=\begin{cases}1,&\text{dist}_{i}\leq\tau_{\text{buf}},\\ \max\!\bigl(\gamma_{\text{min}},\;1-\rho\,(\text{dist}_{i}-\tau_{\text{buf}})\bigr),&\text{dist}_{i}>\tau_{\text{buf}}.\end{cases} (6)

Here τbuf\tau_{\text{buf}} is the tolerance buffer that absorbs week-level misalignments, ρ\rho is the per-day decay rate, and γmin\gamma_{\text{min}} is the floor that keeps distant-yet-relevant evidence from vanishing. When detect=false\texttt{detect}=\text{false}, the temporal channel is closed, and the decay is bypassed, so score​(q,mi)\text{score}(q,m_{i}) reduces to sem​(q,mi)\text{sem}(q,m_{i}). The system takes the top-kk by score as ℰ^\hat{\mathcal{E}} and feeds it to the downstream LLM.

3.3 Reward Design and GRPO Training

The pipeline of Sections 3.1–3.2 is driven by πθ\pi_{\theta}, but zz is discrete and blocks end-to-end gradient flow from the retriever; we therefore train πθ\pi_{\theta} with reinforcement learning. Each training sample carries four gold supervisions: gold_temporal∈{true,false}\texttt{gold\_temporal}\in\{\text{true},\text{false}\}; the gold window set WgoldW_{\text{gold}}, present only when gold_temporal=true\texttt{gold\_temporal}=\text{true}; the gold evidence ℰ∗={ek}k=1|ℰ∗|\mathcal{E}^{*}=\{e_{k}\}_{k=1}^{|\mathcal{E}^{*}|}; and the gold answer a∗a^{*}. Appendix C details the supervision provenance and split construction.

Sparse supervision from answer correctness routr_{\text{out}} alone is insufficient for stable learning of when to trigger the temporal channel and which window to fetch from: a correct answer obtained from a wrong window would still be reinforced by routr_{\text{out}}. We therefore decompose the training signal into four complementary rewards that correspond to different aspects of the retrieval decision: temporal need, window localization, evidence coverage, and answer correctness. With fixed reward weights, these rewards are combined as

R=wdet​rdet+wwin​rwin+wevd​revd+wout​rout,∑∙w∙=1,R=w_{\text{det}}\,r_{\text{det}}+w_{\text{win}}\,r_{\text{win}}+w_{\text{evd}}\,r_{\text{evd}}+w_{\text{out}}\,r_{\text{out}},\qquad\sum_{\bullet}w_{\bullet}=1, (7)

The detection reward rdetr_{\text{det}} supervises whether the temporal channel is correctly triggered, given by the agreement between detect and gold_temporal:

rdet={+1,detect=gold_temporal,−1,otherwise.r_{\text{det}}=\begin{cases}+1,&\texttt{detect}=\texttt{gold\_temporal},\\ -1,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (8)

The window-localization reward rwinr_{\text{win}} measures the geometric alignment of WpredW_{\text{pred}} with WgoldW_{\text{gold}}: for any window pair (P,G)(P,G) we take the IoU φ⁡(P,G)=|P∩G|/|P∪G|\varphi(P,G)=|P\cap G|/|P\cup G|, and aggregate via a symmetric, bidirectional best match. For non-temporal queries or when Wpred=∅W_{\text{pred}}=\emptyset, we set rwin=0r_{\text{win}}=0.

rwin=12​(1|Wgold|​∑G∈WgoldmaxP∈Wpred⁡φ⁡(P,G)+1|Wpred|​∑P∈WpredmaxG∈Wgold⁡φ⁡(P,G)).r_{\text{win}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\!\left(\tfrac{1}{|W_{\text{gold}}|}\!\sum_{G\in W_{\text{gold}}}\max_{P\in W_{\text{pred}}}\varphi(P,G)+\tfrac{1}{|W_{\text{pred}}|}\!\sum_{P\in W_{\text{pred}}}\max_{G\in W_{\text{gold}}}\varphi(P,G)\right). (9)

The evidence reward revdr_{\text{evd}} feeds the retrieval outcome back to the locator: rwinr_{\text{win}} only scores the geometric overlap between WpredW_{\text{pred}} and WgoldW_{\text{gold}}, while revdr_{\text{evd}} checks whether the retriever conditioned on WpredW_{\text{pred}} actually places ℰ∗\mathcal{E}^{*} within top-kk. An independent LLM judge tests, item by item, whether eke_{k} is semantically covered by ℰ^\hat{\mathcal{E}}, and the evidence reward is the coverage rate

revd=1|ℰ∗|​∑k=1|ℰ∗|𝟏​[ek​ covered by ​ℰ^].r_{\text{evd}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{E}^{*}|}\sum_{k=1}^{|\mathcal{E}^{*}|}\mathbf{1}\bigl[e_{k}\text{ covered by }\hat{\mathcal{E}}\bigr]. (10)

The outcome reward routr_{\text{out}} is the direct signal of whether the final answer a^\hat{a} is correct, evaluated per question type:

rout={𝟏​[ExactMatch​(a^,a∗)],multiple-choice,𝟏[majj=1,2,3judge(j)(a^,a∗)=1],open-ended,r_{\text{out}}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{1}\bigl[\mathrm{ExactMatch}(\hat{a},a^{*})\bigr],&\text{multiple-choice},\\ \mathbf{1}\bigl[\mathrm{maj}_{j=1,2,3}\,\mathrm{judge}^{(j)}(\hat{a},a^{*})=1\bigr],&\text{open-ended},\end{cases} (11)

where ExactMatch\mathrm{ExactMatch} checks string equality after normalization, and judge(j)\mathrm{judge}^{(j)} denotes three independent LLM-judge calls whose majority vote suppresses single-evaluation variance. Appendix J.6 audits judge consistency across model families.

A finite annotated (q,detect,Wpred)(q,\texttt{detect},W_{\text{pred}}) set covers neither the long tail of natural-language temporal phrasings nor the actual downstream retrieval and reasoning effects, so we adopt a two-stage scheme of SFT cold-start followed by GRPO online optimization: SFT aligns the locator to a fixed JSON schema and seeds an initial window guess, while GRPO uses RR as the policy-gradient signal to self-correct over end-to-end rollouts,

𝒥(θ)=𝔼q,{z(j)}∼πθold[1G∑j=1Gmin(ρ(j)A(j),clip(ρ(j),1−ϵ,1+ϵ)A(j))]−β𝔻KL(πθ∥πref),\mathcal{J}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{q,\,\{z^{(j)}\}\sim\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}}\!\!\left[\tfrac{1}{G}\sum_{j=1}^{G}\min\!\bigl(\rho^{(j)}A^{(j)},\;\mathrm{clip}\bigl(\rho^{(j)},1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon\bigr)\,A^{(j)}\bigr)\right]-\beta\,\mathbb{D}_{\text{KL}}\!\bigl(\pi_{\theta}\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}\bigr), (12)

Rollouts whose output cannot be parsed by the schema are clamped to R=RminR=R_{\text{min}} and skip the downstream judge; rollouts are U-shape difficulty-stratified by |Wgold||W_{\text{gold}}|.

4 Experiments

4.1 Datasets

LifeBench [4] is a benchmark for long-term, multi-source, fragmented personal memory that spans both declarative and non-declarative memory. It contains one-year synthetic personal histories for ten users, with on average roughly 13,000 entries per user and a total of 2,003 questions spanning five categories: Information Extraction (IE), Multi-hop Reasoning (MR), Nondeclarative Memory Reasoning (ND), Temporal and Knowledge Updating (TKU), and Unanswerable (UA); following the LoCoMo evaluation protocol, the Unanswerable category is excluded from evaluation.

LoCoMo [15] focuses on extremely long multi-session dialogues with QA spanning five reasoning categories—single-hop, multi-hop, temporal, open-domain, and adversarial; following prior work, we evaluate on its 1,540-question subset excluding the adversarial category. Expanded benchmark descriptions and evaluation protocols are provided in Appendix A.

4.2 Experiments Setup

Baselines.

We compare against three families of baselines; aside from Oracle, all methods share the same downstream answer model and top-kk retrieval budget. Agentic memory frameworks: MemOS [12] is a memory operating system that builds unified mechanisms across parametric, activation, and plaintext memory types; TiMem [11] is a temporal-hierarchical memory framework that consolidates conversations into a temporal memory tree for long-horizon agents; Zep [21] is a memory layer service for LLM agents that synthesizes history into a temporally-aware knowledge graph; Mem0 [5] is a memory-centric architecture that extracts, consolidates, and retrieves salient information from ongoing conversations. Time-aware retrieval: TsContriever [28] applies supervised contrastive learning with temporally-constrained negatives to fine-tune the query encoder, routing queries through a classifier to handle temporal constraints. Temporal reasoning: NeSTR [13] performs neuro-symbolic abductive reasoning over symbolic temporal representations with reflection and consistency checking. We do not include training-based temporal-reasoning methods such as Memory-T1 [6] as direct baselines, since they fine-tune the response model, whereas our evaluation keeps the downstream LLM fixed across methods. We additionally report Oracle, which directly provides the gold-evidence context, as a non-comparable upper bound.

Implementation.

The locator πθ\pi_{\theta} uses Qwen3-1.7B [32] as its backbone and is trained with GRPO [23] via the veRL framework [24], with KL coefficient β=0.1\beta=0.1 and group size G=8G=8; the query-adaptive timeline summary 𝒮q\mathcal{S}_{q} fed to πθ\pi_{\theta} is restricted to the top-30 most query-relevant timeline entries for computational efficiency. The semantic channel uses the BGE-M3 [3] dense retriever together with BM25 [22]; the boost coefficient is λboost=0.3\lambda_{\text{boost}}=0.3, and the distance-decay function γ\gamma uses buffer τbuf=14\tau_{\text{buf}}=14, decay rate ρ=0.05\rho=0.05, and floor γmin=0.3\gamma_{\text{min}}=0.3. All methods retrieve top-k=20k=20, except Oracle which directly supplies the gold evidence. The downstream answer model and LLM judge are GPT-5-mini on LifeBench and GPT-4o-mini on LoCoMo, fixed across all baselines for fairness. The evaluation is re-executed three times, and the reported metric is the sample mean ±\pm sample standard deviation across the three runs. The detailed introduction and implementation of baselines can be found in Appendix  E. We evaluate on the user-0 and user-1 split of LifeBench (408 questions) and on the full LoCoMo set; the remaining LifeBench splits (user-2 through user-9) are used to synthesize training samples, so the training and evaluation users on LifeBench are disjoint, while LoCoMo serves as a zero-shot generalization test.

4.3 Results

Main results.

On LifeBench (Table 1, 408 questions) and LoCoMo (Table 2, 1,540 questions), TIDER simultaneously attains the best overall accuracy: 61.52% on LifeBench (second-best NeSTR 52.70%, +8.82+8.82%) and 78.96% on LoCoMo (second-best TiMem 75.30%, +3.66+3.66%); the locator is only 1.7B, far smaller than the shared downstream answer models GPT-5-mini / GPT-4o-mini, confirming that the gain comes from a structured retrieval-time temporal localization rather than from a stronger response model. Compared with agentic-memory frameworks (MemOS, TiMem, Zep, and Mem0), TIDER achieves the best performance on both datasets. On LifeBench, it outperforms the strongest baseline in this group, Mem0 (51.80%), by 9.72%; on LoCoMo, it surpasses the strongest baseline in this group, TiMem (75.30%), by 3.66%. The time-aware retriever TsContriever performs poorly on both datasets, with a substantially larger gap to TIDER on LifeBench than on LoCoMo. This result supports the concern raised in §1: coupling temporal and semantic signals in a shared representation space can weaken semantic recall, especially in large-scale long-term memory settings such as LifeBench, where relative and indirect temporal expressions are more prevalent and place greater stress on encoder-fused retrieval. As a temporal reasoning baseline, NeSTR processes temporal information at the answer stage rather than during retrieval. It underperforms TIDER by 8.82% and 5.48% on LifeBench and LoCoMo, respectively, highlighting the importance of addressing temporal mismatch before evidence enters the downstream context. The effectiveness of TIDER stems from its dual-channel retrieval architecture with explicit window constraints: by moving temporal constraints upstream into the retrieval stage as an explicit window, TIDER suppresses semantically similar but temporally mismatched candidates without degrading semantic recall, offering a structural advantage over both embedding-stage temporal supervision and reasoning-stage post-processing.

Although TIDER achieves the highest overall accuracy on LoCoMo, its Temporal accuracy and token-level F1 are slightly below TiMem’s. Our analysis suggests this gap stems from cross-dataset window-localization mismatch on LoCoMo’s sparser timeline: predicted windows cover 76.25% of gold dates, compared with 93.77% on LifeBench. Using oracle windows raises Temporal accuracy from 71.65% to 79.13% and F1 from 51.72% to 57.83%, surpassing TiMem on both.

Stratified analysis by window count.

To unpack overall accuracy by question type, we stratify the 408 LifeBench questions into four categories (Fig. 3). Time-independent queries form the non-temporal category. For the remaining questions, we segment gold-evidence dates into temporal windows, where any gap of at least three days starts a new window, and group them into single-window, dual-window, and multi-window categories by window count. As shown in Fig. 3, TIDER attains the best accuracy in every category. On non-temporal queries, its margin over the next-best baseline is only 0.67%0.67\%, suggesting that closing the temporal channel does not hurt pure semantic recall. Across the three temporal categories, TIDER improves over the strongest baseline by 9.789.78% on average, with the largest gains arising when evidence must be localized across separated temporal windows (+14.8%), suggesting that long-horizon agent memory benefits from treating temporal cues as an independent retrieval dimension rather than folding them into semantic similarity. Appendix F provides more detailed analysis results with standard deviations. Appendix G.2 provides case studies from different temporal categories, illustrating how baselines can retrieve same-entity events from the wrong time, miss one of two required temporal anchors, or fall back to long-running persona facts, whereas TIDER recovers the correct evidence from long-term memory.

4.4 Ablation Study

Module ablations.

Table 3 reports cumulative ablations of TIDER’s main components. Overall accuracy decreases monotonically from 61.52%61.52\% to 51.45%51.45\% as we remove the distance-decay reranker, the temporal channel, and the timeline summary 𝒮q\mathcal{S}_{q}. Removing the distance-decay reranker reduces Overall accuracy by 3.92%3.92\%, with the largest drop on the time-sensitive TKU category (6.53%6.53\%), which is especially sensitive to temporal alignment. Further removing the temporal channel yields an additional 5.39%5.39\% drop, while removing 𝒮q\mathcal{S}_{q} from the remaining semantic-only setting accounts for another 0.76%0.76\%. F1 shows a non-monotonic trend: removing the temporal channel reduces F1 by 19.4019.40 points, while further removing 𝒮q\mathcal{S}_{q} recovers 15.4315.43 points. This suggests that the timeline summary is most effective when paired with the temporal channel; without temporal constraints, it can introduce noisy context that hurts token-level matching. Overall, TIDER’s gains arise from the coupled operation of the temporal interval locator, the dual-channel retriever, and the distance-decay reranker, rather than from any single component in isolation.

To separate temporal retrieval gains from memory construction, we cross two memory representations with two retrieval methods while keeping all other settings fixed. TIDER improves Overall accuracy over semantic-only retrieval by 8.09% on flat fixed chunks and 9.31% on the full memory pool. Full memory construction adds 1.72% and 2.94% under semantic-only and TIDER retrieval, respectively. These results indicate that TIDER’s gains come primarily from temporal retrieval rather than memory construction. The complete factorial comparison is provided in Appendix D.2.

We also ablate the reward components while keeping the remaining training and retrieval pipeline fixed. Jointly removing the detection reward rdetr_{\text{det}} and window-localization reward rwinr_{\text{win}} reduces Overall accuracy by 5.64% and TKU accuracy by 15.22%. Removing the outcome reward routr_{\text{out}} or evidence reward revdr_{\text{evd}} reduces Overall accuracy by 2.45% or 1.96%, respectively. These results show that the detection and window-localization rewards are particularly important for learning effective temporal retrieval, especially on time-sensitive questions. Detailed results are reported in Appendix C.6.

Locator substitution.

We isolate the locator by fixing the dual-channel retriever and distance-decay reranker (Fig. 4). Removing GRPO from the Qwen3-1.7B locator drops Overall to 55.64%55.64\% (−5.88%-5.88\%, with the largest loss on TKU at −13.05%-13.05\%), while the zero-shot Qwen3-1.7B locator reaches only 53.19%53.19\%, barely above the No-Temporal lower bound (+0.98%+0.98\%), confirming that the temporal path requires a trained window policy. A much larger GPT-5.2 zero-shot locator improves to 57.84%57.84\% but remains −3.68%-3.68\% below TIDER, showing scale alone cannot replace reward-optimized temporal localization. Conversely, an Oracle Window upper bound (WgoldW_{\text{gold}}) adds only +1.70%+1.70\% Overall because TIDER’s predicted windows already cover 93.77%93.77\% of gold dates. These results indicate the temporal path provides the structural capacity, while GRPO learns the window-alignment policy needed to activate it.

Hyperparameter robustness.

We examine TIDER’s sensitivity to retrieval budget, temporal settings, and memory construction on LifeBench (Fig. 5). Each sweep varies one setting while keeping the others fixed. Cells show accuracy differences(%) from the default score, with outlines marking default settings. Detailed results are provided in Appendix D.

Retrieval top-kk. Figure 5(a) varies the number of retrieved memories passed to the answer model. Accuracy changes non-monotonically with the retrieval budget, indicating that retrieving more memories does not consistently improve answer quality. At k=20k=20, TIDER achieves 61.52%61.52\% accuracy, exceeding the best semantic-only result at k=100k=100 by 3.793.79% while retrieving one fifth as many memories. Increasing TIDER’s budget from 2020 to 100100 improves accuracy by only 0.490.49%. These results support k=20k=20 as an effective balance between retrieval volume and answer accuracy.

Temporal settings. Figure 5(b) examines the timeline-input size KK, boost coefficient, decay floor, decay rate, and temporal buffer. Here, KK controls the timeline information supplied to the locator, whereas kk in panel (a) controls the retrieved memories supplied to the answer model. Across the displayed settings, Overall accuracy ranges from 58.45%58.45\% to 61.52%61.52\%. The largest within-sweep variation is 3.07%3.07\%, with only 2.10%2.10\% for the decay floor and 1.86%1.86\% for the buffer. These results demonstrate the robustness of temporal retrieval to hyperparameter choices within the tested ranges.

Memory construction. Figure 5(c) varies the date-merge tolerance, semantic merge threshold, cluster-size cap, and summarizer model. Overall accuracy ranges from 57.84%57.84\% to 63.73%63.73\%, with every tested configuration remaining above the semantic-only baseline of 52.21%52.21\% on the default full memory pool. The construction choices nevertheless affect performance: replacing GPT-4o-mini with GPT-5-mini raises accuracy to 63.73%63.73\%, while reducing the cluster-size cap to 2020 items lowers it to 57.84%57.84\%. Thus, memory construction remains an important design choice.

5 Conclusion

In this work, we introduced TIDER, a time-aware agentic retrieval framework that addresses temporal-mismatch failures at retrieval time, where correct evidence is buried by semantically similar yet temporally mismatched candidates before any downstream reasoner can act on it. At the core of TIDER is a query-adaptive temporal interval locator, decoupled from the semantic encoder, that emits explicit temporal windows. These windows define a parallel temporal channel, whose candidates are merged with semantic candidates and reranked by temporal distance, suppressing temporally mismatched distractors while preserving semantic recall. The locator is trained via GRPO, with a composite reward that balances temporal need, window localization, evidence coverage, and answer correctness. Extensive evaluation on LifeBench and LoCoMo shows that TIDER attains state-of-the-art accuracy with only a 1.7B locator, and locator-substitution analysis confirms that the gain comes from retrieval-time temporal constraints rather than model scale. These results suggest temporal cues are crucial for pinpointing target evidence amid a vast pool of semantically similar historical events in long-term daily-life memory. We discuss limitations and broader impact in Appendix I.

Appendix A Dataset Details

This appendix describes the two long-horizon memory benchmarks used in our evaluation, the categories they expose, the train / evaluation splits we adopt, and the metrics under which all systems are compared.

A.1 LifeBench

LifeBench [4] is a long-horizon multi-source personalized memory benchmark designed to stress-test memory systems beyond chat-only settings. It contains synthetic year-long personal histories for ten users (user-0 through user-9), with on average roughly 13,00013{,}000 entries per user. Each user trace integrates multi-source daily traces—multi-session chat dialogues, phone-operation logs, trip and location histories, exercise and health-tracking records, and free-form personal notes—generated through an anonymized-persona-driven simulator with explicit temporal anchoring and cross-source consistency checks, so semantically similar events recur across the year and force the memory system to disambiguate by time and context. Questions span five categories—Information Extraction (IE), Multi-hop Reasoning (MR), Nondeclarative Memory Reasoning (ND), Temporal and Knowledge Updating (TKU), and Unanswerable (UA)—summing to 2,0032{,}003 items in total, and are answered open-endedly under an LLM-as-judge protocol with GPT-5-mini. State-of-the-art memory systems that score around 90%90\% on prior chat-only benchmarks (e.g., LoCoMo, LongMemEval) drop to 55%55\% overall on LifeBench, confirming that multi-source temporal personal histories pose a substantially harder retrieval and reasoning challenge. Following the LoCoMo evaluation protocol, we exclude UA, which leaves 1,9311{,}931 effective questions. We evaluate on the user-0 / user-1 split (408408 questions after UA exclusion) and synthesize training samples from user-2 through user-9, so the training and evaluation users on LifeBench are disjoint.

A.2 LoCoMo

LoCoMo [15] is a benchmark for very long-term conversational memory: each instance is a multi-session dialogue between two persona-grounded agents that, on average, spans 600600 turns and 1616K tokens across up to 3232 sessions, far exceeding the five-session horizon of prior long-term-dialogue benchmarks. The dialogues are produced by a machine–human pipeline that grounds the speakers in personas and a temporal event graph, with optional image sharing for multi-modal turns and human annotators verifying long-range consistency and event-graph faithfulness. The associated QA benchmark covers five reasoning categories—single-hop, multi-hop, temporal, open-domain, and adversarial—and was designed to expose the difficulty of comprehending long-range temporal and causal dynamics within dialogues. Following prior work, we evaluate on the 1,5401{,}540-question subset after excluding the adversarial category. LoCoMo serves as a zero-shot generalization test: no LoCoMo conversations or questions enter our training pipeline.

A.3 Evaluation Metrics

We evaluate all systems with the official end-to-end question-answering protocol of LoCoMo [15] and LifeBench [4]: Accuracy and F1. This subsection gives the precise definitions and explains why we do not report classical retrieval-side metrics such as Recall@kk as headline numbers.

Accuracy.

For each question qq with gold answer a∗a^{*} and predicted answer a^\hat{a}, we obtain a binary correctness score Acc⁡(q)∈{0,1}\mathrm{Acc}(q)\in\{0,1\} via the official locomo_grader judge prompt (Appendix J.3). To suppress single-evaluation variance, we invoke the same judge prompt three independent times and adopt the majority vote (≥2/3\geq 2/3 correct) as the final label, matching the routr_{\text{out}} definition used during GRPO training (Eq. 11). The judge model is GPT-5-mini on LifeBench and GPT-4o-mini on LoCoMo, fixed across all baselines for fairness; cross-judge variance is audited in Appendix J.6. Answer generation, in contrast, is dataset-specific—LifeBench follows its official QA_PROMPT and LoCoMo follows the Mem0-style ANSWER_PROMPT_MEM0, both reproduced verbatim in Appendix J.3.

F1.

F1 is the token-level harmonic mean of precision and recall between the normalised prediction a^~\tilde{\hat{a}} and the normalised gold a∗~\tilde{a^{*}}, following the standard preprocessing inherited by the LoCoMo reference implementation: lowercasing, article and punctuation removal, and white-space tokenisation.

Why not Recall@kk?

Conventional IR metrics presuppose a canonical evidence unit shared across all systems, against which gold relevance labels can be defined uniformly. The agentic-memory baselines we compare against, as well as TIDER itself, do not consume raw conversations directly: each system ingests the raw data and emits a method-specific memory representation through compression, extraction, or rewriting. These resulting units differ substantially in granularity—from temporally anchored event clusters in TIDER’s memory pool ℳ\mathcal{M} (Eq. 1), to session-level summaries in TiMem [11] and MemoryBank [35], per-utterance dense chunks in TsContriever [28], and temporal knowledge-graph triples in Zep [21]. Consequently, top-kk retrieval results are not directly comparable across systems: a top-kk set of summaries covers substantially more raw evidence than a top-kk set of utterances, and there is no principled normalization that aligns these heterogeneous units. Forcing a single unit, such as raw utterances, would penalize systems whose designs intentionally rewrite or condense memory, thereby conflating memory-construction choices with retrieval quality. We therefore follow the convention established by LoCoMo and LifeBench and evaluate all systems using the same downstream task performance metrics: QA accuracy and F1.

Retrieval Metrics over the Same Memory Pool.

The comparability limitation above concerns systems with heterogeneous memory representations. For a controlled retrieval-side comparison, we additionally evaluate TsContriever, the semantic retriever used as NeSTR input, and TIDER on the same LifeBench memory pool ℳ\mathcal{M}. Because memory entries undergo extraction and rewriting, exact string matching cannot reliably align them with raw gold evidence. We therefore use an LLM coverage judge to assign binary relevance labels. Recall@kk is the fraction of gold evidence covered by the top-kk results, averaged over queries; nDCG@20 measures ranking quality using the binary relevance labels; and MRR@20 is the mean reciprocal rank of the first relevant memory within the top-20 results. These judge-based diagnostics supplement, rather than replace, the end-to-end QA metrics.

Table 4 shows that TIDER improves Recall@20 and nDCG@20 over the shared semantic retriever by 9.019.01 and 11.4611.46 percentage points, respectively. Recall@10 is similar, while the larger Recall@20 and MRR@20 support improved evidence coverage and earlier ranking of relevant memories within the same representation. These results are conditional on the LLM coverage labels and should not be interpreted as representation-independent retrieval scores across native agentic-memory systems.

Appendix B Memory Pool Construction

This appendix details the date extraction, clustering, and summarization steps that turn the raw dialogue 𝒞\mathcal{C} into the temporally anchored event memory pool ℳ\mathcal{M} used by both retrieval channels; the full prompts driving these steps are listed in Appendix J.1.

B.1 Date Extraction and Clustering

Each dialogue turn is processed by an LLM that extracts atomic memory items together with their associated dates. Items are then aggregated into clusters by a temporally-bounded greedy merge: an item joins an existing cluster only when its timestamp falls within Δdate=7\Delta_{\text{date}}=7 days of the cluster span and its semantic similarity (under the same dense retriever as the semantic channel) to the cluster centroid satisfies θsem≥0.85\theta_{\text{sem}}\geq 0.85; clusters are capped at 4040 items each—once a cluster reaches the cap, subsequent items spawn a new cluster even if both temporal and semantic conditions hold. Each surviving cluster ii records its date span di=[distart,diend]d_{i}=[d_{i}^{\text{start}},d_{i}^{\text{end}}], an LLM-generated event summary sis_{i}, and the raw items ℐi\mathcal{I}_{i}.

B.2 Cluster Statistics

We report cluster statistics for all ten LifeBench users (EN). “#Items” counts raw chat turns absorbed by all clusters; “#Clusters” is the total number of LLM-summarized event clusters surviving the merge step described in Appendix B; “Items / cluster (avg)” is the arithmetic mean of cluster sizes; “Timeline span (days)” is the calendar span between the earliest and latest cluster date.

B.3 Locator-Input Timeline Coverage Audit

To check whether the clustered timeline summaries preserve the coarse temporal anchors needed by the locator, we audit the locator’s actual input on the LifeBench user-0 / user-1 slice. For each question, an LLM reviewer receives the gold evidence events and the top-30 timeline summaries locator input, then judges whether those summaries contain enough coarse event-level clues to localize the evidence to the correct temporal window.

Appendix C Locator Training Details

This appendix specifies the training procedure for the locator πθ\pi_{\theta}: the SFT cold-start, the GRPO online phase, the composite-reward weighting, and the difficulty-stratified rollout.

C.1 Training Data Construction

We synthesize training samples from LifeBench user-2 through user-9. For each query qq, we annotate four gold supervisions:

  • •

    gold_temporal∈{true,false}\texttt{gold\_temporal}\in\{\text{true},\text{false}\}, indicating whether the query is time-sensitive.

  • •

    the gold window set WgoldW_{\text{gold}}, present only when gold_temporal=true\texttt{gold\_temporal}=\text{true}.

  • •

    the gold evidence ℰ∗={ek}k=1|ℰ∗|\mathcal{E}^{*}=\{e_{k}\}_{k=1}^{|\mathcal{E}^{*}|}.

  • •

    the gold answer a∗a^{*}.

Annotation provenance.

The four supervisions above originate from heterogeneous sources rather than a single annotation pass.

Gold answer a∗a^{\ast}. Each a∗a^{\ast} is taken verbatim from LifeBench, which ships an authoritative answer for every QA instance: a single option letter (A/B/C/D) for multiple-choice questions and a short reference text for open-ended questions. No filtering or rewriting is applied.

Gold evidence ℰ∗\mathcal{E}^{\ast}. Each LifeBench QA instance carries an evidence_resolved field that lists one record per supporting evidence, with source identifier, type, date, and raw texts. We adopt the field verbatim and convert each record into a (date,text)(\text{date},\text{text}) tuple consumed by the evidence reward revdr_{\text{evd}}.

Gold windows WgoldW_{\text{gold}}. Derived deterministically from the dates in ℰ∗\mathcal{E}^{\ast}. Each evidence date is first cast as a degenerate single-day interval [d,d][d,d]; intervals are then sorted by start date and merged whenever the gap to the previous interval is fewer than three calendar days, otherwise emitted as a new window. Evidence with missing or unparseable dates is skipped. The resulting WgoldW_{\text{gold}} collapses dense evidence clusters into a single tight window and exposes sparse clusters as multi-window targets, providing the natural difficulty stratification used in Appendix C.

Temporal flag gold_temporal. A binary indicator of whether qq is time-sensitive. We obtain an initial label by prompting GPT-5.2 to classify each query in isolation, and a human annotator subsequently verifies every label and overrides the model decision when warranted. This two-stage pipeline reduces both false positives (queries whose evidence happens to carry incidental dates) and false negatives (implicitly temporal queries whose surface form omits explicit time markers).

The resulting set contains 1,5891{,}589 samples spanning the four window-count buckets used by the difficulty-stratified rollout in Appendix C: 3838 non-temporal (|Wgold|=0|W_{\text{gold}}|=0, 2.4%2.4\%), 1,0141{,}014 single-window (|Wgold|=1|W_{\text{gold}}|=1, 63.8%63.8\%), 383383 dual-window (|Wgold|=2|W_{\text{gold}}|=2, 24.1%24.1\%), and 154154 multi-window (|Wgold|≥3|W_{\text{gold}}|\geq 3, 9.7%9.7\%).

C.2 SFT Cold-Start

SFT aligns πθ\pi_{\theta} to the locator output schema (Appendix J) and seeds an initial window guess. Training data are pairs (q,z∗)(q,z^{*}) derived from the gold annotations. We initialize from Qwen3-1.7B–and train for 22 epochs with peak learning rate 2×10−52\times 10^{-5}, per-GPU batch size 44, gradient-accumulation steps 22, and maximum sequence length 61446144 tokens, on 22 GPUs; the effective batch size is therefore 1616.

C.3 GRPO Hyperparameters

For the GRPO objective in Eq. (12), the likelihood ratio for rollout jj is

ρ(j)=πθ​(z(j)∣q,𝒮q)πθold​(z(j)∣q,𝒮q),\rho^{(j)}=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(z^{(j)}\mid q,\mathcal{S}_{q})}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(z^{(j)}\mid q,\mathcal{S}_{q})},

and A(j)A^{(j)} is the group-normalized advantage computed from the composite rewards of the GG rollouts sampled for the same query. This normalization follows GRPO: the rewards within a group are centered and scaled before clipping, while the KL term is applied against the reference policy πref\pi_{\text{ref}}.

C.4 Reward Weights

The composite reward (Eq. (7)) uses weights

wdet=0.10,wwin=0.25,wevd=0.20,wout=0.45,∑∙w∙=1.w_{\text{det}}=0.10,\quad w_{\text{win}}=0.25,\quad w_{\text{evd}}=0.20,\quad w_{\text{out}}=0.45,\qquad\textstyle\sum_{\bullet}w_{\bullet}=1.

The end-task signal woutw_{\text{out}} takes the largest share because answer correctness is the only term that depends jointly on detection, window prediction, and downstream synthesis; the three intermediate weights wdet,wwin,wevdw_{\text{det}},w_{\text{win}},w_{\text{evd}} supply dense supervision early in training, when routr_{\text{out}} is still sparse. Among the intermediate signals, wwin>wevdw_{\text{win}}>w_{\text{evd}} because window-prediction errors propagate to evidence retrieval, so localizing the window is the higher-leverage upstream signal.

For rwinr_{\text{win}} in Eq. (9), the bidirectional IoU score is computed only for temporal samples with nonempty WgoldW_{\text{gold}} and nonempty WpredW_{\text{pred}}. Let 𝒯win\mathcal{T}_{\text{win}} denote the case where gold_temporal=true\texttt{gold\_temporal}=\text{true}, Wgold≠∅W_{\text{gold}}\neq\emptyset, and Wpred≠∅W_{\text{pred}}\neq\emptyset. The full boundary-condition form is:

b⁡(Wpred,Wgold)\displaystyle b(W_{\text{pred}},W_{\text{gold}}) =12​(1|Wgold|​∑G∈WgoldmaxP∈Wpred⁡φ⁡(P,G)+1|Wpred|​∑P∈WpredmaxG∈Wgold⁡φ⁡(P,G)),\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}\!\left(\tfrac{1}{|W_{\text{gold}}|}\!\sum_{G\in W_{\text{gold}}}\max_{P\in W_{\text{pred}}}\varphi(P,G)+\tfrac{1}{|W_{\text{pred}}|}\!\sum_{P\in W_{\text{pred}}}\max_{G\in W_{\text{gold}}}\varphi(P,G)\right),
rwin\displaystyle r_{\text{win}} ={b⁡(Wpred,Wgold),𝒯win,0,otherwise.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}b(W_{\text{pred}},W_{\text{gold}}),&\mathcal{T}_{\text{win}},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Non-temporal samples, empty predictions, and samples whose gold evidence yields no parseable temporal window therefore receive rwin=0r_{\text{win}}=0. This convention avoids undefined maxima or normalizers and leaves the decision of whether the temporal channel should be opened to rdetr_{\text{det}}.

C.5 Difficulty-Stratified Rollout and RminR_{\text{min}}

Rollouts are reweighted by an asymmetric U-shape difficulty-aware reweighting (DAR) schedule indexed by |Wgold||W_{\text{gold}}|: the two extremes of the difficulty axis are up-weighted, while the easier middle buckets are kept at the base weight 1.01.0. The factor for non-temporal questions (×10\times 10) is much larger than that for multi-window questions (×4\times 4) because the non-temporal bucket is severely under-represented in the training distribution (2.4%2.4\% of samples; see Appendix C), whereas the multi-window bucket, while still skewed, is less so (9.7%9.7\%). Concretely:

The effective-probability column applies the DAR factors to the empirical training distribution reported in Appendix C (per-bucket sample counts 38/1,014/383/15438/1{,}014/383/154), then renormalizes. Rollouts whose locator output cannot be parsed by the JSON schema (Appendix J) are clamped to R=Rmin=0R=R_{\text{min}}=0 and bypass the LLM judge.

C.6 Reward-Component Leave-One-Out Ablation

Table 9 reports leave-one-out ablations over the four composite-reward terms of Eq. (7). Each non-full row removes the indicated reward term during the GRPO phase while keeping the SFT cold-start, the locator backbone, the dual-channel retriever, and the downstream LLM fixed. Detection and window-IoU are removed jointly because rwinr_{\text{win}} is gated on rdet=1r_{\text{det}}{=}1.

C.7 Training Curves

Figure 6 plots the per-step reward for three independent GRPO runs that share an identical training recipe and differ only in launch timing. Each dashed curve is one run’s first 300 steps after EMA smoothing (α=0.95\alpha{=}0.95, bias-corrected); the solid line is the per-step mean across the runs—averaging all three for step. The three trajectories are visually superimposed during the early ascent and remain within a narrow band at the plateau, indicating that the GRPO gain reported in §4.3 is reproducible rather than an artifact of a single training trajectory.

C.8 Lightweight Locator: 1.7B vs 4B

Locator capacity is not the source of TIDER’s gains. We re-ran the full TIDER pipeline with a 4B locator under an identical training recipe; only the SFT cold-start and GRPO traces are model-specific, while the dual-channel retriever, prompts, and downstream LLM are unchanged. Figure 7 overlays the smoothed reward of the 4B run on the 1.7B run from Figure 6: the two trajectories rise on a similar shape and converge to plateaus differing by less than 0.020.02 in reward, with the 4B run ascending marginally faster in the early phase. On the evaluation side, Table 10 reports end-to-end accuracy on LifeBench. Halving the locator from 44B to 1.71.7B parameters leaves Overall accuracy and average F1 effectively unchanged (61.5261.52 vs 61.0361.03; 0.69230.6923 vs 0.69570.6957), with per-category swings within ±2.2\pm 2.2 pp. We therefore adopt the 1.71.7B locator as the default, attributing TIDER’s headroom to the dual-channel temporal anchor rather than to locator scale. TIDER thus inherits a lightweight characteristic, achieving competitive end-to-end accuracy under a substantially smaller locator parameter budget.

Appendix D Ablation Study

D.1 Hyperparameter Robustness

This subsection reports the full hyperparameter sweep referenced in §4.4. Across the 2525 configurations summarized in Fig. 8, Overall accuracy stays within a narrow [57.73,61.52]%[57.73,61.52]\% band, far above the No-Temporal bound (52.21%52.21\%). Per-hyperparameter ranges are: λboost\lambda_{\text{boost}} (3.86%3.86\%, most sensitive), top-KK timeline entries (3.14%3.14\%), decay rate ρ\rho (3.14%3.14\%), floor γmin\gamma_{\text{min}} (2.10%2.10\%), buffer τbuf\tau_{\text{buf}} (1.86%1.86\%, most stable). The chosen defaults sit at or near each per-panel optimum, and a single shared configuration applies across both LifeBench evaluation users without per-user tuning.

D.2 Memory Construction–Retrieval Factorial Comparison

To separate the effects of memory construction and retrieval, we cross two memory representations with two retrieval methods on LifeBench. The fixed-chunk representation uses 512-token chunks with timestamps inherited from their source sessions, without LLM-based extraction, clustering, rewriting, or summarization; the locator directly consumes the timestamped chunks. The full representation uses the temporally anchored memory pool ℳ\mathcal{M}. Within each representation, we compare semantic-only retrieval with TIDER retrieval while holding the downstream answer model and retrieval budget fixed.

TIDER improves accuracy by 8.098.09 percentage points on fixed chunks and 9.319.31 points on the full memory pool. Memory construction adds 1.721.72 points under semantic retrieval and 2.942.94 points under TIDER retrieval. The retrieval-time mechanism therefore remains effective without LLM-based memory construction, while the full memory pool provides an additional, retrieval-dependent benefit.

D.3 Retrieval Top-kk Sweep

We vary the number of retrieved memory units passed to the answer generator, kk, while fixing the memory pool, answer generator, and all other settings. This retrieval budget differs from the top-KK timeline-input size in Appendix D.1, which controls the information supplied to the locator.

Accuracy varies non-monotonically with kk. Increasing the semantic retrieval budget narrows the gap, but the best semantic-only result within the tested range is 57.73%57.73\% at k=100k=100, still 3.793.79 percentage points below TIDER at k=20k=20 (61.52%61.52\%). Increasing TIDER’s budget from 2020 to 100100 improves accuracy by only 0.490.49 points. These results support k=20k=20 as an effective operating point: TIDER achieves higher accuracy than the best tested semantic-only setting while retrieving one fifth as many memory units. This comparison concerns memory-unit counts, not measured token costs or end-to-end latency.

D.4 Memory-Construction Hyperparameter Sweep

We vary the date-merge tolerance Δdate\Delta_{\text{date}}, semantic merge threshold θsem\theta_{\text{sem}}, cluster-size cap, and summarizer model individually, keeping the other settings at their defaults. The default construction uses Δdate=7\Delta_{\text{date}}=7 days, θsem=0.85\theta_{\text{sem}}=0.85, a cap of 4040 items, and GPT-4o-mini as the summarizer. Table 13 reports the corresponding LifeBench Overall accuracies.

Accuracy ranges from 59.07%59.07\% to 61.76%61.76\% for Δdate\Delta_{\text{date}}, 59.56%59.56\% to 61.52%61.52\% for θsem\theta_{\text{sem}}, 57.84%57.84\% to 61.52%61.52\% for the cap, and 60.29%60.29\% to 63.73%63.73\% across summarizer models. All tested configurations remain above the default full-pool semantic-only accuracy of 52.21%52.21\%. This comparison supports robustness relative to that reference operating point.

Appendix E Baseline Details

This appendix expands the one-line baseline descriptions in §4.2 and details the implementation choices that ensure a fair comparison.

E.1 Method Summaries

We group the six baselines into three families along their orthogonal design dimensions: agentic memory frameworks (MemOS, TiMem, Zep, Mem0) that target memory organization and lifecycle management, time-aware retrieval (TsContriever) that targets the retrieval encoder, and temporal reasoning (NeSTR) that targets answer-time inference over retrieved evidence. The summaries below paraphrase each paper’s stated contribution; the closing line marks what we preserve from the original method versus what we adapt to keep the comparison on equal footing with TIDER.

MemOS [12] treats memory as a manageable system resource and proposes a memory operating system that unifies the representation, scheduling, and evolution of plaintext, activation-based, and parameter-level memories. Its basic unit, the MemCube, encapsulates memory content together with provenance and versioning metadata; MemCubes can be composed, migrated, and fused over time, bridging retrieval-style memory with parameter-based learning under explicit lifecycle control. Adapted: the downstream answer model is replaced by our shared LLM (GPT-5-mini on LifeBench, GPT-4o-mini on LoCoMo) so that gains attributable to memory organization are isolated from the choice of generator.

TiMem [11] is a temporal–hierarchical memory framework that organizes conversations through a Temporal Memory Tree (TMT), enabling systematic memory consolidation from raw observations to progressively abstracted persona representations. It is characterized by three properties: temporal–hierarchical organization through TMT, semantic-guided consolidation that integrates memory across hierarchical levels without fine-tuning, and complexity-aware memory recall that balances precision and efficiency across queries of varying complexity. Adapted: the downstream answer LLM is unified with the rest of the table, leaving TiMem’s memory tree as the only varying component.

Zep [21] is a memory-layer service for AI agents whose core component, Graphiti, dynamically synthesizes unstructured conversational data and structured business data into a temporally-aware knowledge graph that maintains historical relationships with explicit validity intervals. Zep was originally evaluated on Deep Memory Retrieval (DMR) and LongMemEval, where it improves over MemGPT and shows substantial gains on cross-session synthesis and long-term context maintenance with reduced response latency. Adapted: the answer model is unified across baselines.

Mem0 [5] is a scalable memory-centric architecture that dynamically extracts, consolidates, and retrieves salient information from ongoing multi-session conversations, with an enhanced graph-based variant that captures relational structure among conversational elements. On the LOCOMO benchmark Mem0 reports a 26%26\% relative improvement over an OpenAI memory baseline under LLM-as-Judge while reducing p95 latency by 91%91\% and saving more than 90%90\% of token cost. Adapted: the downstream answer LLM and top-kk retrieval budget are unified.

TsContriever [28] (a.k.a. TS-Retriever) is a time-sensitive retrieval-augmented generation method built on top of Contriever. It augments dense retrieval with supervised contrastive learning using temporally-constrained negatives, performs query-side fine-tuning to make the encoder sensitive to explicit temporal expressions, and routes queries through a temporal-need classifier so that general queries fall back to standard semantic retrieval. The original paper reports clear gains on a custom time-sensitive QA benchmark while preserving general-query effectiveness. Adapted: We preserve the four official checkpoints (plain, document, query, router) and the routing classifier. We disable the TIDER locator and plug TsContriever into our shared memory pool, retrieval pipeline, top-kk, and answer LLM, so the difference reflects the encoder change alone.

NeSTR [13] is a Neuro-Symbolic Temporal Reasoning framework that integrates structured symbolic representations of temporal relations with hybrid reflective reasoning to enhance LLMs’ temporal sensitivity. It explicitly preserves temporal relations through symbolic encoding, enforces logical consistency through verification, and corrects flawed inferences via abductive reflection, achieving zero-shot gains on temporal QA benchmarks without any fine-tuning. Adapted: We preserve the NeSTR for response generation, including symbolic temporal encoding, consistency verification, and abductive reflection. We disable TIDER’s locator, temporal grounding and temporal reranker at the search stage, share the memory pool and dense retriever.

E.2 Excluded Baselines

We do not include training-based temporal-reasoning methods such as Memory-T1 [6] as direct baselines, since they fine-tune the response model whereas our evaluation keeps the downstream LLM fixed across methods.
