Appendix G Diagnostic Analysis and Case Studies

This appendix analyzes why methods fail on LifeBench. We first summarize LLM-judged error causes over incorrect answers (§G.1), then provide qualitative case studies covering single-, dual-, and multi-window queries (§G.2).

G.1 Error-Cause Analysis

For each incorrect answer, we ask an LLM reviewer to assign exactly one primary error cause by comparing the question, gold answer, model answer, gold evidence, and retrieved context (Appendix J.5). The labels are: retrieval miss, where the answer-bearing evidence is absent; temporal mismatch, where related evidence is retrieved from the wrong time; partial evidence, where only part of the required evidence is retrieved; and reason failure, where sufficient evidence is present but the answer model reasons or selects incorrectly. We define retrieval-side failure as the union of retrieval miss, temporal mismatch, and partial evidence.

Table 16 shows that most failures are retrieval-side rather than pure answer-generation failures. Temporal mismatch is the dominant failure type for MemOS, Mem0, NeSTR, and TIDER, while TiMem and TsContriever still exhibit many retrieval misses, indicating that their retrievers often fail before temporal disambiguation can help. Overall, the diagnosis supports the paper’s central claim: long-horizon memory QA is bottlenecked by retrieving the right evidence from the right time, not merely by answer-time reasoning.

G.2 Case Studies

We summarize the recurring baseline failure modes observed across cases and then walk through three representative cases covering single-, dual-, and multi-window queries.

Common baseline failure modes.

Baseline mistakes fall into five recurring patterns: (i) topic shell only—retrieved context preserves the right person and broad theme but loses the specific event core (e.g., MemOS, Zep on q100, q181); (ii) event substitution with temporal drift—a same-person event from a nearby month replaces the queried one (e.g., TiMem and Mem0 on q100, q181); (iii) long-term persona suppression—high-frequency identity facts override the question’s specific temporal window (e.g., MemOS and TsContriever on q143); (iv) single-endpoint capture—one of two required temporal anchors is retrieved while the other is dropped (e.g., MemOS, NeSTR on q120, q193); and (v) near-total miss—retrieval finds little relevant content (e.g., TsContriever on q100, q164). The three walk-throughs below illustrate (i)–(iv); failure mode (v) is largely confined to TsContriever and is consistent with its low overall accuracy in Table 14.

Case 1: same-entity multi-event disambiguation (user0/q100).

The question asks what trouble Huang Wenhui ran into in March 2025; the gold answer is that her pre-sold apartment project halted construction amid rumors that the developer’s cash flow had broken down. Within the same conversational thread, Huang Wenhui appears in at least five negatively-toned events spread across the year—a January cafe scam (q181), the March apartment halt, an April game-project conflict (q28), April/July neighbor-dog disturbances (q98, q37), and a September app-launch slump (q49)—so the challenge is isolating the March incident from this same-entity cluster. TIDER retrieves the March 12 messages that explicitly mention the halted construction site, the broken developer cash flow, and the continuing mortgage pressure. MemOS and Zep keep only the topic shell (“A-Hui has a housing problem”); TiMem replaces the event with a later apartment-water-leak story; Mem0 drifts to the July neighbor-dog incident; NeSTR preserves the negative-affect shell but slides to the January cafe scam. All baselines identify the correct entity, but only TIDER recovers the correct month-event pair.

Case 2: dual-window endpoint coverage (user1/q120).

The question asks for the user’s core activities on the first weekend after moving (June 14–15). The gold answer requires a complete two-day chain: a park walk and a housewarming dinner on day one, then a Pilates session and a pottery-class breakthrough on day two. TIDER retrieves evidence for all four components, with both days’ messages co-occurring in its retrieved context, and answers the chain completely. MemOS retains the park-walk fragment but drops the second-day activities; TiMem and Zep pull in broadly related “new-home” or “weekend” memories without preserving the precise two-day structure; NeSTR captures the park and pottery pieces but misses Pilates. The challenge here is not topical relevance but preserving every answer-bearing endpoint required by a temporally compositional question.

Case 3: stage-level multi-window summarization (user1/q143).

The question asks what the user’s main work content was at Zhengzhou Central Hospital between August 11 and August 27; the gold answer is a respiratory-medicine rotation, including community-acquired pneumonia admissions, a COPD exacerbation case, a difficult-case discussion meeting, and the associated discharge documentation. TIDER’s retrieved context anchors the August 11 admission and initial-course record, the August 21 case-discussion presentation, and the August 27 differential-diagnosis preparation, and additionally surfaces a “reviewing the respiratory medicine section” note. MemOS, Zep, and TsContriever all collapse back to the user’s long-running cardiology persona (resident physician, cardiology rounds, cardiology case work), missing the temporary respiratory rotation entirely; TiMem fails to retrieve a coherent August 11–27 chain; Mem0 surfaces individual clinical actions but drops the rotation-stage label. This case illustrates how high-frequency persona evidence can override a specific time-bounded stage, and how TIDER’s window-anchored retrieval resists this drift.

Appendix H Computational Resources

H.1 Training Cost

We separate the SFT cold-start (Appendix C.2) from the GRPO main loop (Appendix C.3). All training uses NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs and the veRL framework. The SFT cold-start consumes about 3 wall-clock hours on 2×2\timesA100 80GB; a single GRPO run trains for 300300 steps in roughly 100 hours on 2×2\timesA100 80GB.

H.2 Inference Latency

We measure the marginal latency introduced by TIDER’s temporal channel on the LifeBench-EN test split, holding the GPT-5-mini answer step fixed and toggling only the temporal pathway. The 1.7B locator is served on a single A100 80GB via vLLM. Averaged across 408408 questions, enabling the temporal channel adds 0.410.41s of wall-clock latency per query relative to the no-temporal baseline; this overhead aggregates the locator forward pass, the timeline-summary retrieval branch, and the distance-decay rerank that fuses the two channels. The figure is well below the cost of the downstream answer call, which dominates end-to-end response time at the several-second scale, so the dual-channel design recovers the accuracy gap reported in Section 4 without bottlenecking the GPT-5-mini / GPT-4o-mini answer step.

Appendix I Limitations and Broader Impact

I.1 Limitations

We discuss three limitations of TIDER that are visible from the current setup and shape the most natural next steps; each isolates a distinct failure axis (data realism, upstream memory dependency, language coverage) so that the relative weight of remediation effort is clear to the reader.

Synthetic personal histories.

LifeBench is generated by an anonymized-persona-driven simulator with explicit temporal anchoring and cross-source consistency checks, and LoCoMo is multi-session synthetic dialogue rather than real long-term user data. Real personal traces likely contain heavier noise, more frequent timestamp gaps, and stronger cross-source contradictions than either benchmark exposes. Validating TIDER on a real, consented personal-memory corpus—under the privacy and retention safeguards discussed in Appendix I.2—therefore remains an open direction, and the gains we report should be read as upper bounds achievable when the temporal signal is well-formed.

Upstream memory-item dependency.

TIDER’s temporal channel operates on a query-adaptive timeline summary 𝒮q\mathcal{S}_{q} drawn from clustered memory items in the memory pool ℳ\mathcal{M} (Appendix B). We deliberately keep this construction as simple as possible—temporally bounded clustering followed by a single-pass summarization prompt—so that the locator does not couple to a bespoke memory representation; even so, 𝒮q\mathcal{S}_{q} still inherits the quality of upstream item extraction, since mis-dated, mis-attributed, or fragmented items propagate into the cluster boundaries and into the resulting summary. The locator can only filter on this view, so its window predictions degrade whenever the upstream memory pool is noisy.

Language scope.

LifeBench and LoCoMo are both English-only, so TIDER’s evaluation does not cover languages whose date conventions diverge from the Gregorian numerical form (e.g., Chinese lunar dates, Japanese era names) or whose temporal expressions carry richer morphological cues. The locator prompt and the gold-window construction both rely on the parser shipped with our extractor, which is calibrated for English; cross-lingual deployment will likely require multilingual date normalization upstream of the temporal channel before the locator’s window predictions become meaningful.

I.2 Broader Impact

TIDER targets long-term personalized assistants whose factual grounding rests on a temporally anchored memory pool; we discuss its societal impact along three positive axes and two risk axes, and note one experimental safeguard. On the positive side: (i) the dual-channel design strengthens the reliability of long-term personal-assistant deployments that must reason over months or years of dialogue history; (ii) by filtering candidates against query-relevant temporal windows rather than reweighting them after generation, the temporal channel directly reduces cross-time evidence hallucinations at the retrieval stage; and (iii) the locator’s window predictions WpredW_{\text{pred}} are user-inspectable, exposing which time region the system treated as relevant and giving end users an auditable handle on retrieval decisions. Two principal risks remain: (i) an adversary who can write into the dialogue stream may craft contradictory or fabricated dates that push the locator toward an incorrect window, thereby suppressing or surfacing specific memories at retrieval time; and (ii) any bias in the upstream LLM-based extractor—including event misattribution along demographic or linguistic lines—propagates directly into the temporally bounded clusters and the resulting timeline summary 𝒮q\mathcal{S}_{q}, so locator decisions inherit those biases without an independent corrective step. As an experimental safeguard, all training and evaluation in this paper use synthetic benchmarks (LifeBench, LoCoMo); no real consented personal-memory corpus was used at any stage.

Appendix J Prompt Templates and Judge Validation

This appendix lists the prompts used by the memory pool builder, the locator, and the two LLM judges in the exact form fed to the underlying LLMs (§J.1–§J.4), and reports a cross-judge consistency audit (§J.6).

J.1 Memory Pool Construction Prompts

The two prompts that drive memory-pool construction are listed below.

Cluster summarization (REORGANIZE_PROMPT).

Used to merge the items in a temporally bounded cluster (or sub-cluster) into a single chronologically-ordered event summary, with date extraction and entity disambiguation handled inline.

⬇
You are a memory clustering and summarization expert.
Given the following child memory items:
{memory_items_text}
Please perform:
1. Identify information that reflects user’s experiences, beliefs,
concerns, decisions, plans, or reactions – including meaningful
input from assistant that user acknowledged or responded to.
2. Resolve all time, person, and event references clearly:
- Convert relative time expressions (e.g., "yesterday," "next Friday")
into absolute dates using the message timestamp if possible.
- Clearly distinguish between event time and message time.
- If uncertainty exists, state it explicitly (e.g., "around June
2025," "exact date unclear").
- Include specific locations if mentioned.
- Resolve all pronouns, aliases, and ambiguous references into full
names or identities.
- Disambiguate people with the same name if applicable.
3. This summary is a navigation aid for retrieval, not canonical
evidence. You may use third-person for clarity, but do not rewrite
into a polished narrative. Do not collapse distinct event instances
across different dates into one fact. Do not introduce any detail
not present in the child items.
4. Do not omit any information that user is likely to remember.
- Include all key experiences, thoughts, emotional responses, and
plans – even if they seem minor.
- Prioritize completeness and fidelity over conciseness.
- Do not generalize or skip details that could be personally
meaningful to user.
5. Summarize all child memory items into one memory item.
Output format requirements:
- The value field must be a natural language paragraph, describing
events in chronological order.
- Absolutely forbidden to output JSON arrays, lists, or structured data
formats (e.g., [{…}, {…}]).
- Each independent event starts with "YYYY-MM-DD," followed by a
sentence. Sentences are separated by periods.
Language rules:
- The ‘key‘, ‘value‘, ‘tags‘, ‘summary‘ fields must match the mostly
used language of the input memory items.
- Keep ‘memory_type‘ in English.
Return valid JSON:
{
"key": <string, a concise title of the ‘value‘ field>,
"memory_type": <string, "LongTermMemory" or "UserMemory">,
"value": <natural language paragraph describing events in
chronological order; preserve dates, amounts, names,
locations; do not collapse different event instances into
one abstract statement; do not introduce facts not present
in the child items>,
"tags": <list of relevant thematic keywords>,
"summary": <natural paragraph from user’s perspective, 120-200 words,
same language as the input>
}

Sub-cluster split.

Used to subdivide an oversized cluster into 2–10-item sub-clusters before summarization.

⬇
You are a memory organization expert.
You are given a cluster of memory items, each with an ID and content.
Your task is to divide these into smaller, semantically meaningful
sub-clusters.
Instructions:
- Identify natural topics by analyzing common time, place, people, and
event elements.
- Each sub-cluster must reflect a coherent theme that helps retrieval.
- Each sub-cluster should have 2-10 items. Discard singletons.
- Each item ID must appear in exactly one sub-cluster or be discarded.
No duplicates are allowed.
- All IDs in the output must be from the provided Memory items.
- Return strictly valid JSON only.
Example: If you have items about a project across multiple phases,
group them by milestone, team, or event.
Language rules:
- The ‘key‘ fields must match the mostly used language of the
clustered memories.
Return valid JSON:
{
"clusters": [
{"ids": ["<id1>", "<id2>", …], "key": "<concise memory title>"},
…
]
}
Memory items:
{joined_scene}

J.2 Locator Prompt and Output Schema

The locator πθ\pi_{\theta} emits a single JSON object with two fields per query: a temporal-sensitivity flag and a list of temporal windows.

⬇
{
"detect": true | false,
"windows": [
{"start": "YYYY-MM-DD", "end": "YYYY-MM-DD"}, …
]
}

The detect field follows the temporal-sensitivity definition listed below, which is the prompt fed to GPT-5.2 to label gold_temporal during training-data construction (Appendix C); πθ\pi_{\theta} is trained to imitate this judgment. The prompt text itself uses the detect key so that the annotation format matches the locator schema. Window prediction is supervised directly from (q,Wgold)(q,W_{\text{gold}}) pairs and does not require a separate LLM prompt template at data-construction time.

⬇
You are a temporal constraint detector. Determine whether the user’s
question requires searching memories within a specific time range.
## What is a temporal constraint
A temporal constraint limits the time range for memory retrieval. Two
types:
- Explicit: directly mentions time, e.g. "in June 2025", "last month",
"during Spring Festival", "in the last 3 days"
- Implicit: indirectly limits time via events, e.g. "after mom got
sick", "before moving", "after that business trip"
- Event-pair (time gap): asks how long between two events – both
events are implicit constraints; extract the events, NOT the time-gap
word ("how long", "how many days")
## What is NOT a temporal constraint (important)
- Factual questions: "When is the birthday", "What time do you wake up"
– asking for information, not limiting search range
- Pure semantic questions: "favorite restaurant", "how do you commute"
- Dates in multiple-choice options (e.g. "A. Jan 6 B. Jan 8") are
answer choices, not search constraints
- Time words that don’t change meaning if removed: "the restaurant
mentioned before" – "before" is casual speech, not a constraint
- Time-gap words are NOT expressions: "how many days", "how long",
"how far in advance" are the answer target – do NOT put them in
expressions
## Expression extraction rules
1. Every temporal expression must be extracted separately – do not
omit any.
2. Explicit dates (e.g. "June 2025", "April 26", "Spring Festival")
must never be omitted, even when other expressions like "recently"
are also present.
3. Do NOT merge time words with event content – "recently changed
jobs" yields "recently", not "recently changed jobs".
## Decision method
Ask yourself: does answering this question require limiting the search
to a specific time period? If not, it’s false.
## User question
${query}
Output strict JSON only (no other text):
{
"detect": true/false,
"expressions": []
}
Fill expressions with the original temporal expressions extracted from
the query. Empty array if no constraint.
## Examples
### Positive (explicit)
Input: In May 2025, what did Zhang Ming’s cat eat?
Output: {"detect": true,
"expressions": ["In May 2025"]}
### Positive (multiple temporal expressions)
Input: In June 2025, Zhang Ming mentioned on the phone that he
recently changed jobs. What was the new job?
Output: {"detect": true,
"expressions": ["In June 2025", "recently"]}
### Positive (implicit)
Input: What pets did he get after moving?
Output: {"detect": true,
"expressions": ["after moving"]}
### Negative (factual question)
Input: What is Zhang Ming’s favorite restaurant?
Output: {"detect": false, "expressions": []}
### Negative (dates in options)
Input: When did Zhang Ming go to the hospital? A. Jan 6 B. Jan 8
C. Jan 10
Output: {"detect": false, "expressions": []}
### Positive (event anchors, not time words)
Input: How many days before checking in did she book the guesthouse?
Output: {"detect": true,
"expressions": ["book the guesthouse", "checking in"]}
### Positive (event-pair time gap)
Input: How many days passed between Zhang Ming signing the lease and
actually moving in?
Output:
{
"detect": true,
"expressions": ["signing the lease", "actually moving in"]
}

J.3 LLM Judge for Answer Correctness (routr_{\text{out}})

Answer generation and answer judging are kept separate. The downstream answer is generated by a frozen LLM, but the answer-generation prompt is dataset-specific: following the LifeBench paper’s official evaluation requirement, LifeBench uses the official QA_PROMPT from the LoCoMo reference implementation, whereas LoCoMo uses the Mem0-style ANSWER_PROMPT_MEM0. In both datasets, answer correctness is judged with the official LoCoMo prompt reproduced below; we invoke the same judge prompt independently three times and use majority vote (CORRECT in at least two of three calls) as the final label.

LifeBench answer generation.

For LifeBench, the retrieved context is prepended before this prompt suffix.

⬇
Based on the above context, write an answer in the form of a short
phrase for the following question. Answer with exact words from the
context whenever possible.
Question: {} Short answer:

LoCoMo answer generation.

The following Mem0-style answer prompt is used for LoCoMo, not for LifeBench.

⬇
You are an intelligent memory assistant tasked with retrieving accurate
information from conversation memories.
# CONTEXT:
You have access to memories from two speakers in a conversation. These
memories contain timestamped information that may be relevant to
answering the question.
# INSTRUCTIONS:
1. Carefully analyze all provided memories from both speakers
2. Pay special attention to the timestamps to determine the answer
3. If the question asks about a specific event or fact, look for
direct evidence in the memories
4. If the memories contain contradictory information, prioritize the
most recent memory
5. If there is a question about time references (like "last year",
"two months ago", etc.), calculate the actual date based on the
memory timestamp. For example, if a memory from 4 May 2022 mentions
"went to India last year," then the trip occurred in 2021.
6. Always convert relative time references to specific dates, months,
or years. For example, convert "last year" to "2022" or "two months
ago" to "March 2023" based on the memory timestamp. Ignore the
reference while answering the question.
7. Focus only on the content of the memories from both speakers. Do
not confuse character names mentioned in memories with the actual
users who created those memories.
8. The answer should be less than 5-6 words.
# APPROACH (Think step by step):
1. First, examine all memories that contain information related to
the question
2. Examine the timestamps and content of these memories carefully
3. Look for explicit mentions of dates, times, locations, or events
that answer the question
4. If the answer requires calculation (e.g., converting relative time
references), show your work
5. Formulate a precise, concise answer based solely on the evidence
in the memories
6. Double-check that your answer directly addresses the question
asked
7. Ensure your final answer is specific and avoids vague time
references
{context}
Question: {question}
Answer:

Answer-correctness judge.

⬇
[system]
You are an expert grader that determines if answers to questions match
a gold standard answer
[user]
Your task is to label an answer to a question as ’CORRECT’ or ’WRONG’.
You will be given the following data:
(1) a question (posed by one user to another user),
(2) a ’gold’ (ground truth) answer,
(3) a generated answer
which you will score as CORRECT/WRONG.
The point of the question is to ask about something one user should
know about the other user based on their prior conversations.
The gold answer will usually be a concise and short answer that
includes the referenced topic, for example:
Question: Do you remember what I got the last time I went to Hawaii?
Gold answer: A shell necklace
The generated answer might be much longer, but you should be generous
with your grading - as long as it touches on the same topic as the
gold answer, it should be counted as CORRECT.
For time related questions, the gold answer will be a specific date,
month, year, etc. The generated answer might be much longer or use
relative time references (like "last Tuesday" or "next month"), but
you should be generous with your grading - as long as it refers to
the same date or time period as the gold answer, it should be counted
as CORRECT. Even if the format differs (e.g., "May 7th" vs "7 May"),
consider it CORRECT if it’s the same date.
Now it’s time for the real question:
Question: {question}
Gold answer: {gold_answer}
Generated answer: {response}
First, provide a short (one sentence) explanation of your reasoning,
then finish with CORRECT or WRONG.
Do NOT include both CORRECT and WRONG in your response, or it will
break the evaluation script.
Just return the label CORRECT or WRONG in a json format with the key
as "label".

J.4 LLM Judge for Evidence Coverage (revdr_{\text{evd}})

The evidence-coverage judge revdr_{\text{evd}} is a reward that measures item-level evidence recall: for each question, the reviewer independently checks every gold evidence item and returns revd=m/nr_{\text{evd}}=m/n, where nn is the number of gold evidence items and mm is the number of items explicitly covered by the retrieved memory set ℰ^\hat{\mathcal{E}}. The reward is therefore a floating-point value in [0,1][0,1].

Evidence-coverage judge.

⬇
[system]
You are a strict evidence-coverage reviewer.
Given a list of gold evidence facts and retrieved memories, decide
what fraction of gold evidence facts are covered by the retrieved memories.
Coverage criteria (strict):
- Each gold evidence fact is judged independently.
- A gold fact is covered only if at least one retrieved memory
explicitly mentions semantically identical content.
- The retrieved text must mention the gold fact’s specific person
names, places, events, numbers, dates, and key modifiers.
- Conceptually related text, partial hits, loose paraphrases, and
superordinate substitutions do NOT count as coverage.
- Synonyms are allowed.
For example, "xiao-long-bao" = "steamed soup dumplings".
- Category broadening is not allowed.
For example, "xiao-long-bao" != "dim sum".
- Missing a key modifier counts as not covered.
For example, "Li Ming ate xiao-long-bao" !=
"Li Ming ate something".
Compute:
coverage = number of covered gold facts / total number of gold facts
Return only JSON in this format:
{
"coverage": <float between 0.0 and 1.0>,
"reason": "<one short English sentence>"
}
Positive 1:
gold:
["Li Ming ate xiao-long-bao in Lujiazui, Shanghai"]
retrieved:
["I went with Li Ming to try xiao-long-bao in Lujiazui,
Shanghai – it was delicious"]
output:
{
"coverage": 1.0,
"reason": "the food and location are identical"
}
Negative 1, superordinate substitution:
gold:
["Li Ming ate xiao-long-bao in Lujiazui, Shanghai"]
retrieved:
["Li Ming ate dim sum in Shanghai"]
output:
{
"coverage": 0.0,
"reason": "dim sum is not equal to xiao-long-bao"
}
Negative 2, partial coverage:
gold:
[
"Li Ming went to Shanghai on April 1",
"Li Ming ate xiao-long-bao in Shanghai"
]
retrieved:
["Li Ming went to Shanghai on April 1 for a meeting"]
output:
{
"coverage": 0.5,
"reason": "only the Shanghai trip on April 1 is covered"
}
Negative 3, number mismatch:
gold:
["Li Ming spent 200 yuan on a book"]
retrieved:
["Li Ming bought a book"]
output:
{
"coverage": 0.0,
"reason": "the price is missing"
}
[user]
gold_evidence:
{gold}
retrieved_memories:
{retrieved}
Output JSON following the rules above.

J.5 Error-Cause Judge Prompt

The following prompt is used for the LLM reviewer in Appendix G.1.

⬇
[system]
You are a strict retrieval failure diagnosis reviewer for
long-horizon personal-memory QA.
Role:
You diagnose why an incorrect answer happened. Your main focus is
retrieval quality, especially whether retrieval selected evidence from
the wrong time or wrong event instance.
Task:
Given one incorrect QA case, compare:
1) question,
2) gold answer,
3) model answer,
4) gold evidence,
5) retrieved context.
Assign exactly one primary_error.
Allowed labels:
1. temporal_mismatch
Use when the retrieved context contains a salient distractor that is
semantically related to the question but temporally incompatible with
the gold evidence. This requires at least one of:
- same person/entity/topic, but a clearly different date/window/event
instance than the gold evidence;
- stale state or old preference used when the question requires a later
updated state;
- future plan/reminder/preview used instead of the actual completed
event;
- long-term persona or routine activity replacing a temporary
time-bounded stage;
- model answer is visibly based on a retrieved wrong-time event.
2. partial_evidence
Use when retrieved context contains correct evidence from the right
event/window but misses other necessary correct evidence. Typical cases:
one hop of a multi-hop query, one endpoint of a dual-window query, one
item in a list, or correct event but missing a key detail.
3. retrieval_miss
Use when the answer-bearing evidence is absent and there is no explicit
wrong-time same-entity/same-topic distractor. This includes off-topic
retrieval, generic persona summaries, vague related memories without a
date/event-instance conflict, and near-empty contexts.
4. reason_failure
Use when retrieved context contains enough correct evidence from the
right event/window to answer correctly, but the model answer is wrong
due to reasoning, aggregation, option selection, or wording.
5. other
Use only when none of the above fits.
Decision procedure:
Step 1: Is there enough correct retrieved evidence from the right
event/window for a careful reader to answer? If yes and answer is still
wrong, choose reason_failure.
Step 2: Is some correct right-event/right-window evidence present but
incomplete? If yes, choose partial_evidence unless a wrong-time
distractor is clearly dominant.
Step 3: Is there an explicit wrong-time/stale/future/wrong-stage
distractor related to the same entity/topic and likely driving the wrong
answer? If yes, choose temporal_mismatch.
Step 4: Otherwise choose retrieval_miss.
Important constraints:
- Do NOT label temporal_mismatch just because the benchmark is temporal.
- Do NOT label temporal_mismatch for non-temporal questions unless the
failure truly depends on stale/updated state or a wrong event instance.
- Do NOT label temporal_mismatch when retrieved context is merely
broad/generic and lacks a clear wrong date/window/event.
- The explanation for temporal_mismatch must name the wrong-time
distractor type, e.g., "July dog incident replaces March apartment
halt" or "cardiology persona replaces August respiratory rotation".
Example A: temporal_mismatch
question: "What trouble did Huang Wenhui face in March?"
gold evidence: "2025-03-12: her pre-sold apartment project halted
construction and the developer’s cash flow broke down."
retrieved context: "2025-07-10: Huang Wenhui complained about a
neighbor’s dog disturbing her sleep."
model answer: "A neighbor’s dog bothered her."
output: {"primary_error":"temporal_mismatch",
"secondary_errors":["retrieval_miss"],
"retrieval_contains_core_evidence":false,
"retrieval_contains_wrong_time_related_evidence":true,
"explanation":"the July dog incident replaces the queried March
apartment halt"}
Example B: retrieval_miss, not temporal_mismatch
question: "What trouble did Huang Wenhui face in March?"
gold evidence: "2025-03-12: her pre-sold apartment project halted
construction."
retrieved context: "Huang Wenhui has been stressed about housing and
work."
model answer: "She had general housing stress."
output: {"primary_error":"retrieval_miss","secondary_errors":[],
"retrieval_contains_core_evidence":false,
"retrieval_contains_wrong_time_related_evidence":false,
"explanation":"the context is generic and lacks a specific wrong-time
event"}
Example C: partial_evidence
question: "What did she do on both days of the first weekend after
moving?"
gold evidence: ["Saturday: park walk and housewarming dinner",
"Sunday: Pilates and pottery class"]
retrieved context: "Saturday: she took a park walk and had a
housewarming dinner."
model answer: "She walked in the park and had dinner."
output: {"primary_error":"partial_evidence","secondary_errors":[],
"retrieval_contains_core_evidence":true,
"retrieval_contains_wrong_time_related_evidence":false,
"explanation":"the correct weekend is retrieved but only the Saturday
endpoint is covered"}
Example D: reason_failure
question: "Which option is the appointment date?"
gold evidence: "The app notification confirmed January 10."
retrieved context: "The app notification confirmed the appointment on
January 10."
model answer: "B: January 8."
output: {"primary_error":"reason_failure","secondary_errors":[],
"retrieval_contains_core_evidence":true,
"retrieval_contains_wrong_time_related_evidence":false,
"explanation":"the right evidence is present but the option selection
is wrong"}
Return only valid JSON:
{
"primary_error": "temporal_mismatch | partial_evidence | retrieval_miss | reason_failure | other",
"secondary_errors": ["temporal_mismatch | partial_evidence | retrieval_miss | reason_failure | other"],
"retrieval_contains_core_evidence": true/false,
"retrieval_contains_wrong_time_related_evidence": true/false,
"explanation": "one concise English sentence"
}
[user]
question:
{question}
gold_answer:
{gold_answer}
model_answer:
{model_answer}
gold_evidence:
{gold_evidence}
retrieved_context:
{retrieved_context}

J.6 Judge Consistency Audit

This appendix audits the variance of the LLM judges used for GRPO.

To audit cross-model agreement, we re-evaluate the same response set (n=408n=408 from LifeBench user-0 and user-1) with two additional judges drawn from different model families—claude-sonnet-4-6 (Anthropic) and gemini-3.1-flash-lite-preview-nothink (Google)—using the exact same system and user prompts as the gpt-5-mini judge reported in the main paper.

gpt-5-mini claude-sonnet-4-6 gemini-3.1-lite
gpt-5-mini — 0.894 0.836
claude-sonnet-4-6 0.894 — 0.894
gemini-3.1-lite 0.836 0.894 —

All three pairwise Cohen’s κ\kappa values lie in [0.836,0.894][0.836,0.894], well above the 0.810.81 threshold conventionally interpreted as “almost perfect” agreement. We therefore report a single judge (gpt-5-mini) throughout the main paper without loss of generality.

NeurIPS Paper Checklist

  1. 1.

    Claims

  2. Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?

  3. Answer: [Yes]

  4. Justification: The abstract and introduction state the TIDER framework, the RL-trained temporal interval locator, the dual-channel retrieval mechanism, and the reported gains on LifeBench and LoCoMo. These claims are supported by the main results in Section 4.3 and ablations in Section 4.4.

  5. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper.

    • •

      The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.

    • •

      The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.

    • •

      It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.

  6. 2.

    Limitations

  7. Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?

  8. Answer: [Yes]

  9. Justification: Appendix I.1 discusses limitations from synthetic personal histories, dependence on upstream memory-item extraction, and English-only evaluation.

  10. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.

    • •

      The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.

    • •

      The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.

    • •

      The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.

    • •

      If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.

    • •

      While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.

  11. 3.

    Theory assumptions and proofs

  12. Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof?

  13. Answer: [N/A]

  14. Justification: The paper proposes an empirical retrieval framework and does not claim theoretical results requiring formal proofs.

  15. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results.

    • •

      All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced.

    • •

      All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.

    • •

      The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition.

    • •

      Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.

    • •

      Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.

  16. 4.

    Experimental result reproducibility

  17. Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)?

  18. Answer: [Yes]

  19. Justification: Sections 4.1–4.2 and Appendices A, B, C, and J describe the datasets, splits, memory-pool construction, training procedure, hyperparameters, prompts, and evaluation protocol needed to reproduce the main results. The supplementary Markdown guide and anonymized code package provide executable scripts and configuration files for reproducing the main results.

  20. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.

    • •

      If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

    • •

      Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.

    • •

      While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example

      1. (a)

        If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm.

      2. (b)

        If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully.

      3. (c)

        If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset).

      4. (d)

        We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results.

  21. 5.

    Open access to data and code

  22. Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material?

  23. Answer: [Yes]

  24. Justification: We provide an anonymized supplementary code package with a Markdown reproduction guide, including environment setup, data preparation instructions, configuration files, and scripts for reproducing the main experiments.

  25. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code.

    • •

      Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

    • •

      While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark).

    • •

      The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

    • •

      The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc.

    • •

      The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why.

    • •

      At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable).

    • •

      Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted.

  26. 6.

    Experimental setting/details

  27. Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results?

  28. Answer: [Yes]

  29. Justification: Section 4.2 specifies datasets, baselines, retrieval budget, model choices, split construction, and key hyperparameters; Appendix C gives SFT and GRPO training details, and Appendix E details baseline adaptation. The supplementary code package includes the corresponding configuration files and run scripts.

  30. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them.

    • •

      The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material.

  31. 7.

    Experiment statistical significance

  32. Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments?

  33. Answer: [Yes]

  34. Justification: The main result tables report means and standard deviations over independent evaluation runs, and Appendix F reports stratified accuracy with standard deviations.

  35. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper.

    • •

      The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions).

    • •

      The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.)

    • •

      The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors).

    • •

      It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean.

    • •

      It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified.

    • •

      For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates).

    • •

      If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text.

  36. 8.

    Experiments compute resources

  37. Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments?

  38. Answer: [Yes]

  39. Justification: Appendix H reports training hardware, wall-clock cost, and the per-query inference latency.

  40. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage.

    • •

      The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute.

    • •

      The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper).

  41. 9.

    Code of ethics

  42. Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines?

  43. Answer: [Yes]

  44. Justification: The work uses synthetic benchmarks and does not use real personal-memory data; privacy and misuse risks are discussed in Appendix I.2. The submission is anonymized and does not disclose identifying author information.

  45. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics.

    • •

      If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics.

    • •

      The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction).

  46. 10.

    Broader impacts

  47. Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed?

  48. Answer: [Yes]

  49. Justification: Appendix I.2 discusses positive impacts for long-term personalized assistants as well as risks from fabricated dates, biased extraction, and propagation of upstream memory errors.

  50. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed.

    • •

      If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact.

    • •

      Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations.

    • •

      The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster.

    • •

      The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology.

    • •

      If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML).

  51. 11.

    Safeguards

  52. Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)?

  53. Answer: [N/A]

  54. Justification: The paper does not release a high-risk foundation model, scraped dataset, image generator, or real personal-memory corpus. As an experimental safeguard, all training and evaluation use synthetic benchmarks.

  55. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks.

    • •

      Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters.

    • •

      Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images.

    • •

      We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort.

  56. 12.

    Licenses for existing assets

  57. Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected?

  58. Answer: [Yes]

  59. Justification: Existing assets used in the paper, including LifeBench, LoCoMo, Qwen3-1.7B, BGE-M3, BM25, veRL, and API-based LLMs, are credited through citations in the paper. The supplementary Markdown guide lists their project links, versions when available, and license or terms-of-use information, and our use follows those terms.

  60. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets.

    • •

      The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset.

    • •

      The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include a URL.

    • •

      The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset.

    • •

      For scraped data from a particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided.

    • •

      If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of a dataset.

    • •

      For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided.

    • •

      If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the asset’s creators.

  61. 13.

    New assets

  62. Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets?

  63. Answer: [Yes]

  64. Justification: We introduce an anonymized supplementary code package as a new asset. It is documented with a Markdown guide describing its purpose, setup, reproduction commands, dependencies, and license.

  65. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets.

    • •

      Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc.

    • •

      The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used.

    • •

      At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file.

  66. 14.

    Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects

  67. Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)?

  68. Answer: [N/A]

  69. Justification: The work does not conduct crowdsourcing experiments or human-subject studies. The only human involvement described is verification of synthetic benchmark-derived temporal labels, not collection of human-subject data.

  70. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects.

    • •

      Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper.

    • •

      According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector.

  71. 15.

    Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects

  72. Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained?

  73. Answer: [N/A]

  74. Justification: The paper does not involve human-subject research or real personal-memory data, so IRB approval is not applicable.

  75. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects.

    • •

      Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper.

    • •

      We recognize that the procedures for this may vary significantly between institutions and locations, and we expect authors to adhere to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and the guidelines for their institution.

    • •

      For initial submissions, do not include any information that would break anonymity (if applicable), such as the institution conducting the review.

  76. 16.

    Declaration of LLM usage

  77. Question: Does the paper describe the usage of LLMs if it is an important, original, or non-standard component of the core methods in this research? Note that if the LLM is used only for writing, editing, or formatting purposes and does not impact the core methodology, scientific rigor, or originality of the research, declaration is not required.

  78. Answer: [Yes]

  79. Justification: LLMs are core components of the method and evaluation: they are used for memory-item extraction and summarization, temporal-label construction, downstream answer generation, and LLM-based judging. These uses are described in Sections 3–4.2 and Appendix J.

  80. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the core method development in this research does not involve LLMs as any important, original, or non-standard components.

    • •

      Please refer to our LLM policy in the NeurIPS handbook for what should or should not be described.
